coherence.reasons: Both run the same logical chain: enter via Amazon, reject retail-led on the board's own tests, payback depends on ad cost, reset the $40M, gate retail at 20% awareness. X organises it around an explicit test of the CEO's hypothesis (five conditions, each with a verdict), and its governing thought, summary, slide titles and four decisions map one-to-one. Its decisions follow from its findings: because payback fails above 28.6% ACoS, it asks the board to restate the payback target. Y has an internal tension. It headlines that A 'passes every financial test in the plan case', then tells the board to plan on 30–32% ACoS, a basis on which its own table shows payback failing. It never turns that into an explicit request to relax the payback constraint. Its stop trigger (ACoS above 32%) also sits well above its own 28.6% break-even. X has one slip: 'A beats B on every board test' contradicts its own table, where both miss the ambition and B is closer. Y's storyline is otherwise clean and well ordered.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (Amazon-led with gates, reset the $40M, retail only at 20% awareness or more with a test), and both weigh Japan honestly as safer but small. X's recommendation is more defensible on the constraints. It states plainly that payback by 2030 holds only at ACoS of 28.6% or less, and asks the board to accept slippage to 2032 inside a $5M envelope. Its gates tighten toward the break-even (ACoS ≤30% at Gate 1, ≤29% at Gate 2, tracked monthly against 28.6%). It defines a hold mode with about $2.5M at risk. It sets retail gates on awareness, Amazon profitability and a measured halo, not before 2030. Y's gates are looser and partly inconsistent with its own analysis. The stop trigger only fires at ACoS above 32% for two quarters, so the plan could run at 29–32%, missing payback, without triggering anything. The tariff checkpoint says to 'absorb it' on the plan case, without noting that at the pilot's 28% ACoS a 25% duty already breaks payback. Y has a useful 'what would change our view' section and frames the Japan trade-off well ('J is the only option that pays back in every case'), but it leaves the payback constraint unresolved instead of putting the trade-off to the board.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key calculations correctly: unit contribution of $4.73 / $4.01 / $3.05 on Amazon and $7.55 in retail, B's peak of $20.8M, B's 2027 group margin of 4.5%, A's cumulative cash of +2.4 / +0.4 / –2.3, the 28.6% break-even ACoS, and the 17.3% CAGR. Both reject the $5.2B figure, the correlation-based halo and the 4.5 units/door assumption, and both note the survivorship in Saebom against the two stalled brands. X goes further on the critical evidence. It gives the break-even ACoS under a 25% duty (26.9%) and shows the pilot case turning negative (–0.7). It re-runs B on evidence-based inputs (–22.9, –26.4, –31.1). It calculates the halo retail would need to pay for itself (2.2–2.6×). It models the CEO's 2029 retail add (6.8% margin, –$9.6M). It also checks whether the pilot trajectory supports 300k units. Y adds volume sensitivities (–20%, break-even 27.0% at –10% volume) and B without the halo ($24.3M), but keeps 4.5 units/door in the model and does not show the tariff-plus-pilot-ACoS case. X's errors are small: 'Japan is ahead on cash unless ACoS stays at or below 28%' is wrong (at 28%, A is +0.4 against J's +1.8), and 'beats B on every test' is overstated. Its post-2030 payback years rest on extrapolation, which it flags. Y's errors are also small: 'Amazon is where most of it is bought' when the share is 41%, and a tariff checkpoint that reasons from the 25% ACoS case it has itself called an upside.

revision.reasons: The key expects 'keep with conditions': keep the Amazon-led route, add gates, reset the $40M. Both do this and both raise the retail trigger from 15% to 20% using the Table 8 band median of 3.5 against the 4.0 delisting line. X handles the hypothesis more rigorously. It breaks it into five testable conditions, marks which hold, hold in part or fail, and models the second half of the CEO's plan as written (600 doors in 2029). That shows it would breach the margin floor (6.8%) and leave cash at –$9.6M by 2030, a finding Y does not have. X then replaces the calendar trigger with evidence gates: awareness on the right base, Amazon profitability, and a measured halo from a regional test. Y keeps the hypothesis with 'four changes' (ACoS basis, cash envelope, 20% gate, door test first). That is appropriate, but it does not quantify what the CEO's retail step would do to the constraints, and it leaves the 2029 retail gate timing largely intact.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach the defensible conclusion on essentially the same model, and both avoid the main traps: market-based sizing, accepting 4.5 units/door or 25% ACoS, the halo correlation, and the $5.2B figure. X serves the board better for three reasons. It turns the conflict between payback and ad cost into an explicit decision: restate the payback and revenue targets. It supplies gates tied to the break-even ACoS, including the tariff-adjusted break-even. And it stress-tests both Option B on realistic inputs and the CEO's own 2029 retail step against the margin floor and payback. Y is tighter and has a good 'what would change our view' section and a candid framing of Japan. But its stop trigger is looser than its own break-even, its tariff checkpoint is reasoned from the optimistic case, and it leaves the payback constraint implicitly breached rather than put to the board. X's minor misstatements (the Japan cash comparison at 28% ACoS, and 'every board test') do not change its conclusions.
